opus-5.5.text:
I think it's helpful to separate two things people often blur together: proving and discovering. A lot of the recent excitement has been about proving — you give a system a well-posed statement, and it searches for a formal proof that a verifier like Lean can check. That's hard, but at least the target is fixed. Conjecture generation is a different kind of problem, because nobody hands you the target. You have to decide what's worth asking in the first place.

How can a system do that? Honestly, it can borrow a lot from how mathematicians already work. Much discovery starts with data and patterns. You compute lots of examples, look at tables, notice that two quantities seem related, and then try to state that as a precise claim. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture came partly out of early computer experiments on elliptic curves. More recently there have been machine learning collaborations on knot invariants and representation theory, where a model picked up a relationship that humans then turned into a theorem. So one route is: generate structured mathematical data at scale, let models find regularities, and then turn those into candidate statements.

The step people underestimate is filtering. Generating conjectures is easy — you can produce millions of true-but-boring statements, or plausible-but-false ones. What matters is interestingness. A good conjecture is surprising, it compresses many observations into one idea, it connects areas that seemed unrelated, and ideally it's within reach of current tools but not trivially so. I think a discovery system needs a tight loop: propose a statement, test it hard against counterexamples, try to prove it or partial cases formally, and use what happens to update its sense of what's fruitful. Formal verification really matters here, because it gives you a ground truth signal that informal reasoning doesn't. You can't fool Lean.

As for breaking through existing boundaries — I'd be a bit careful. Early on, the most realistic progress isn't a machine inventing a new field from nothing. It's a system that's tireless at exploring the neighborhood of known mathematics, much more widely than any person can, and spotting things humans missed because nobody had time to check them all. Over time, if the system can also build new definitions, new abstractions that make hard problems easier, that's where it starts to look like real creativity. A lot of the great leaps in math weren't new theorems so much as new concepts — the right definition can make a hundred hard results suddenly natural.

So my picture is a collaboration. The machine handles enormous search, verification, and pattern finding. Humans bring taste, motivation, and the sense of why a question matters. And I suspect the systems will gradually learn some of that taste too, by seeing which conjectures turned out to be deep and which were dead ends. That feedback loop, grounded in formal proof, is what I find most exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that generating conjectures is actually the hard part, much harder than proving things once you know what to prove. A lot of the excitement around AI and math has been about proof, about taking a stated theorem and finding a formal argument for it. That matters, and systems have gotten genuinely good at it. But the thing that makes a mathematician great isn't really proving. It's taste. It's knowing which question is worth asking in the first place.

So when I think about how a system can generate conjectures, I break it into a few pieces.

The first is pattern detection at scale. Mathematicians have always done this by hand. Gauss stared at tables of primes and guessed the prime number theorem decades before anyone could prove it. Ramanujan filled notebooks with identities he found by computation and intuition. A system today can run millions of experiments, compute invariants across huge families of objects, and notice correlations a human would never have the time or patience to see. That's a real capability, and it already works in places like knot theory, combinatorics, and number theory.

But the second piece is where it gets interesting, and that's filtering. If you ask a model to generate conjectures, it will happily give you thousands. Most will be trivially true, trivially false, or true but boring. The thing we care about is the statement that is surprising and yet turns out to be right. So you need some notion of what "interesting" means, and I think that comes from connecting two areas that didn't obviously talk to each other, or from a statement that would simplify a lot of existing results if true. We're starting to see systems that can be trained on that signal, and formal verification helps enormously because you can at least throw out everything that's false before a human ever looks at it.

The third piece, breaking boundaries, is the one I'm most cautious and most hopeful about. Most of the time, a model trained on existing mathematics will produce conjectures that live inside existing mathematics. That's useful but it's not a breakthrough. The genuinely new thing happens when a system is allowed to search in a space humans haven't explored, with a verifier in the loop to tell it when it's actually found something. Reinforcement learning against a formal checker gives you that. The system can wander into strange territory, and the checker keeps it honest. Some of the first results from that approach are statements no one had written down because no one had thought to look there, not because they were deep.

What I'd push back on is the idea that this replaces mathematicians. I think it changes what the job is. The mathematician becomes the person who decides which of these conjectures is worth a career, who interprets what a strange true statement means, and who builds the theory around it. That's a more human job, not a less human one. And frankly, it's the part most of us got into mathematics for in the first place.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make conjecture generation part of a feedback loop. A system explores examples, notices a pattern, proposes a statement, and then tries both to prove it and to find a counterexample. A failed attempt can be productive: it may reveal a missing assumption or suggest a stronger underlying structure.

The harder question is what makes a conjecture interesting. You can generate many statements that are true but don’t explain very much. We want systems that identify ideas that connect apparently separate problems, simplify an argument, or give us a useful new definition. So checking correctness is essential, but it isn’t enough to guide discovery.

To break through existing boundaries, I think these systems need room to change the representation of a problem. Rather than only asking, ‘Can I prove this statement with the tools I have?’ they should also ask, ‘Is there another way to formulate this that makes the structure clearer?’ That’s where collaboration with mathematicians could be especially valuable: the system can explore possibilities, while the human helps assess which directions have mathematical significance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to connect generating conjectures with trying to prove them. A system can look at examples and propose patterns, but a pattern alone isn’t enough. You want it to ask: What assumptions are actually necessary? Can I find a counterexample? Does this connect to something we already understand?

That creates a feedback loop. If a proof attempt fails, the failure might suggest a missing condition or a more useful definition. If a counterexample appears, it can help sharpen the conjecture. So even unsuccessful attempts can move the mathematics forward.

To break through existing boundaries, though, these systems need some way to judge which questions are worth pursuing. Producing thousands of true statements is different from finding one that changes how we understand a subject. I think a promising direction is collaboration: systems can explore possibilities and check arguments, while mathematicians help identify the questions and connections that carry deeper significance. Over time, that interaction could also teach us something about mathematical taste itself.
